title: Why does a digit’s place matter?
answer: In 342, the 3 means three hundreds, the 4 means four tens, and the 2 means two ones. The same digit can be worth a different amount in another place. In 432, the 3 means three tens. You can build these numbers with bundles of sticks. A hundred bundle holds ten bundles of ten, and a ten bundle holds ten single sticks. You can swap ten loose sticks for one ten bundle.
facts: In our number system, each place is worth ten times the place immediately to its right.

title: What does zero do in a number?
answer: Zero can tell you that there is none of something. An empty basket has zero apples. It also helps show where other digits belong. In 205, the zero shows that there are no tens between the two hundreds and the five ones. If you leave out the zero, 25 means two tens and five ones. Zero is on the number line too, between negative and positive numbers.
facts: Adding zero leaves a number the same.

title: How do you round a number?
answer: Rounding replaces a number with a nearby number that is easier to say or use. To round 47 to the nearest ten, look at 40 and 50. It is seven away from 40 and three away from 50, so 47 rounds to 50. A number exactly halfway between two tens needs an agreed rule. In the usual school rule for whole numbers, 45 rounds up to 50. This rule helps everyone report the same rounded answer.
facts: Rounding 47 to the nearest ten and nearest hundred gives different answers.

title: How can you estimate an answer?
answer: An estimate is a sensible guess based on what you know. Suppose you are adding 29 stickers, 42 stickers, and 38 stickers. They are close to 30, 40, and 40, so you can guess there are about 110. That tells you whether you need a small envelope or a bigger box. If you must give every student the same number of stickers, you can count the exact total before sharing.
facts: An estimate can help you spot an answer far from the right size.

title: How do rows help you multiply?
answer: Imagine setting out three rows of four buttons. Each row has the same number, so you can count by fours or multiply three by four. There are twelve buttons. Turn the arrangement sideways and you see four rows of three. There are still twelve. A neat arrangement in equal rows and columns is called an array. Arrays let you see that switching the two numbers in a multiplication gives the same total.
facts: Three groups of four and four groups of three each total twelve.

title: What is left over after division?
answer: Think of giving seventeen markers to four people. Give each person one, then repeat as long as everyone can get another. Each person gets four markers, and one marker is left. The marker left over is the remainder. What you do with it depends on the question. For markers you can leave one in the box. If you are sharing a cake, you could cut the piece you have left into smaller pieces.
facts: In whole-number division, the remainder must be smaller than the number you divide by.

title: What makes a number even or odd?
answer: Put your socks into pairs. If each sock gets a partner, the number of socks is even. If one sock is left without a partner, the number is odd. Fourteen is even and fifteen is odd. Zero is even, because it leaves no sock without a partner. When you look at a whole number written in our usual digits, the last digit tells you whether you can put it into pairs.
facts: A whole number ending in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8 is even.

title: What are factors?
answer: Two numbers that multiply to make a whole number are a pair of factors of that number. For twelve, picture rows of buttons. You can make one row of twelve, two rows of six, or three rows of four. These are three different factor pairs for twelve. Arrange the same buttons in five equal rows and some will be left over, so five is not a factor of twelve.
facts: The positive factors of twelve are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12.

title: What are multiples?
answer: Count by threes, starting at three. You get 3, 6, 9, 12, and so on. Each of these numbers is a multiple of three because it holds a whole number of groups of three. Zero is also a multiple of three, since it holds zero groups. When you look at a list of multiples of four, some numbers will appear on both lists. Twelve is on both, so it is a common multiple.
facts: Every positive whole number is a multiple of one.

title: What is a prime number?
answer: Try arranging seven counters in a rectangle with no gaps. You can make one row of seven or seven rows of one, but you cannot make equal rows with both sides greater than one. Seven is prime because its only positive factors are one and seven. Six can make two rows of three, so it is not prime. One is not prime either, since it has just one positive factor.
facts: Two is the only even prime number.

title: What does the decimal point show?
answer: In 4.36, the decimal point sits between the ones place and the parts smaller than one. The 4 stands for four ones. The 3 just after the point stands for three tenths, and the 6 farther right stands for six hundredths. Imagine a dollar split into a hundred pennies. Four dollars and thirty-six pennies can be written as $4.36. The decimal point stays after the whole dollars.
facts: Writing 0.5 or 0.50 gives the same number.

title: What does percent mean?
answer: Percent means out of a hundred. Imagine a square marked with a hundred little boxes. If you shade fifty boxes, you shaded 50 percent. That is the same amount as one half of the big square. A hundred percent covers the whole square, and zero percent covers none of it. You can use percent to compare parts of groups even when the groups have different sizes.
facts: A quarter is 25 percent because 25 is one fourth of 100.

title: What are numbers below zero?
answer: You can picture numbers on a line, with zero near the middle. Positive numbers are to the right, and negative numbers are to the left. The number minus three is three steps left of zero. Numbers below zero are handy for things like temperatures on a cold night. A thermometer at minus six degrees reads colder than one at minus two degrees, even though six by itself is larger than two.
facts: Moving right along a number line gives you larger numbers.

title: How do you measure around a shape?
answer: The perimeter is the distance all the way around a flat shape. Picture a rectangular garden that is six steps long and four steps wide. Walk around its edge, and you go six steps, then four, then six, then four. That makes twenty steps. Measuring the space inside the garden would tell you its area. Perimeter tells you how much fencing might go around it.
facts: If all four sides are five meters long, the perimeter is twenty meters.

title: How do you measure the space inside a box?
answer: Volume tells you how much three-dimensional space something takes up. Imagine fitting small cubes into a rectangular box. One layer of three rows of four cubes holds twelve cubes. If two layers fit, the box holds twenty-four cubes. Using a cube of a known size, such as one cubic centimeter, gives you a way to describe the amount of space. Bigger cubes would give a smaller count.
facts: The space in a rectangular box can be found by multiplying its inside length, width, and height, using the same unit.

title: What makes an angle wide or narrow?
answer: An angle shows how far one direction turns from another. Open a book a little. The covers make a narrow angle, smaller than a square corner. Open it until one cover points straight up while the other lies flat. That is a right angle. Open it farther and the angle becomes wider. The amount of turn can change even if both parts of the book are the same size.
facts: A right angle measures 90 degrees.

title: How does a protractor measure a turn?
answer: A protractor is a tool with numbers marked around part of a circle. Put its center on the point where the two sides of an angle meet, and line its zero mark up with one side. Follow the other side to see which number it reaches. If the tool has two rows of numbers, choose the row that begins at the zero you lined up. A narrow angle should give a number below ninety.
facts: A half-circle protractor measures turns from zero to 180 degrees.

title: How are triangles different from one another?
answer: Every triangle has three straight sides and three corners. Some triangles have three equal sides. Others have just two equal sides, or all three sides have different lengths. You can also group triangles by their corners. A right triangle has one square corner, like the corner of a sheet of paper. Each way of sorting helps you describe the same shape in a different way.
facts: The three inside angles of any flat triangle add up to 180 degrees.

title: Is every square a rectangle?
answer: To be a rectangle, a flat shape must have four straight sides and four right angles. A square has all of those things. It has an extra property too: all four sides have the same length. A long postcard is usually a rectangle with two long sides and two short sides, so it is not a square. You can think of a square as one special kind of rectangle.
facts: A square has four sides of the same length, and every corner is a right angle.

title: What are the radius and diameter of a circle?
answer: A circle is made of points all the same distance from a center. Draw a straight line from the center to the edge. That line is a radius. Extend that line back through the center until it reaches the opposite edge. The full line across is a diameter, twice as long as the radius. The distance around the curved edge has a different name: circumference.
facts: If the radius is three centimeters, the diameter is six centimeters.

title: How far is it around a circle?
answer: Wrap a thread once around the outside of a flat round lid and measure the thread. That gives its circumference. Now measure straight across the lid through the center to find its diameter. The thread is a little longer than three diameters. For every exact circle, the ratio of those lengths is the same. Mathematicians call that number pi, often rounded to 3.14.
facts: A circle with twice the diameter also has twice the circumference.

title: What makes two halves match?
answer: Draw a heart, then imagine folding it down the middle. If every part of one half lands on the same part of the other half, the fold is a line of symmetry. A shape can have more than one matching fold. A square matches across a fold through the middle from side to side, and also across a fold joining opposite corners. Some shapes have no matching fold at all.

title: How can you predict the next part of a pattern?
answer: Read these colors aloud: red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue. The smallest block that keeps repeating is red, blue, blue. If that rule continues, the next color is red. Seeing only a few colors does not always tell you the rule for sure. Another person might be following a different rule that begins the same way. Looking for a repeating block gives you a guess you can check against more of the pattern.

title: How does a number machine work?
answer: A number machine is a way to picture a rule. Put in a number, follow the same rule each time, and see what number comes out. If the rule is to add three, an input of two gives an output of five, and an input of four gives seven. A two-step rule could first double the input and then add one. In that rule the order matters.

title: Which part of a calculation comes first?
answer: If you see 2 + 3 × 4, you might think to add first. In the usual order of operations, multiplication comes before addition, so three times four is twelve and the total is fourteen. Put parentheses around 2 + 3 and the instructions change. Do what is inside the parentheses first, then multiply five by four, to get twenty. The symbols let everyone read the calculation the same way.
facts: Multiplication and division have the same rank. When they appear together at that rank, work from left to right.

title: How do you find one point on a grid?
answer: On a simple grid, start where the two number lines meet. The first number in an ordered pair tells you where to go sideways. The second tells you where to go up or down. For the point (3, 2), go three steps right and two steps up. Negative numbers take you left or down instead. Switching the order changes the point. That is why the numbers always go in the same order.
facts: On a first-quadrant grid, the starting point is (0, 0), called the origin.

title: How do bars show data?
answer: A bar graph uses bars to show how much is in each group. Imagine surveying a class about favorite fruit. A bar for apples can reach six, a bar for bananas might reach four, and one for grapes eight. Read the group labels and check the numbered scale before comparing the bars. One mark on a scale might stand for one vote, two votes, or another amount.

title: What does the mean tell you?
answer: Imagine three friends have two, four, and twelve marbles. Altogether they have eighteen. If they share those eighteen marbles equally, each gets six. Six is the mean of the three original numbers. It helps tell you how much each person would have if the total were shared evenly, even when the real amounts are very different. The mean can fall between numbers in your list.

title: How do you find the median?
answer: Put the numbers 2, 6, 7, 10, and 50 in order from smallest to largest. The number in the middle is seven. That is the median. Changing 50 to an even larger number would leave the middle number right where it is. When there are two middle numbers, find the amount halfway between those two. That is the median of the whole list. Ordering the numbers first is what makes the comparison work.
facts: The median of 2, 4, 8, and 12 is 6, halfway between 4 and 8.

title: How likely is something to happen?
answer: Probability tells how likely an event is. A fair coin has two equally likely sides, so the chance it lands heads is one half. That does not say what will happen on the next toss. You might get heads three times in a row. Over many tosses, the share of heads often comes closer to one half. A different game with more possible results might have very different chances.
facts: In a game with equally likely outcomes, a probability of zero means impossible and a probability of one means certain.

title: How do meters, centimeters, and kilometers fit together?
answer: A meter is a unit of length. A centimeter is one hundredth of a meter, so a meter stick has a hundred centimeters along it. A kilometer is a thousand meters, a useful unit for a trip across town. These units belong to the metric system. Their sizes are related by tens, hundreds, or thousands, so you can switch between units by working with powers of ten.

title: How do watercolors make light colors?
answer: With watercolors, a brush carries small bits of color mixed with water. A thin layer lets light reach the white paper and bounce back, so the paper helps the color look bright or pale. Artists can brush water over a large area before adding color to make it spread softly. When one layer dries, they can paint over it to build a stronger color or add sharp lines.

title: What makes a picture a collage?
answer: A collage is made by arranging pieces of material on a surface and attaching them. The pieces might be colored paper, scraps of cloth, photographs, or something else. A strip from an old map could become a roadway in a new picture, even though it once showed a river. Artists decide how edges overlap and where to leave empty space. title: How is a sculpture different from a drawing?

A sculptor can carve away parts of a block, add pieces of clay, or join materials together. Some sculptures have a flat back and rise from a wall or a plaque, so you usually look at them from one side.

title: What is a still life in art?
answer: A still life is an artwork about objects such as a bowl, a book, flowers, or fruit. An artist can put the objects close to one another so their shapes overlap, or spread them out so we notice each one. Moving the light to one side can make the shadows longer and change which details stand out. Even the same cup can look different when you move your chair and draw it from a new place.

title: What is a landscape painting?
answer: A landscape artwork shows a view of a place. It might show hills, a river, fields, or a busy town. The part that seems nearest is the foreground, and the part that seems farthest is the background. An artist can use large, clear shapes close to us and smaller, softer ones farther away. answer: Mosaics use small pieces of glass, stone, or another material arranged into a picture or pattern. Each piece can cover just a little bit of the final surface. title: How does weaving turn threads into cloth?
answer: A weaver stretches one set of threads in order. Those threads are the warp. Another thread, the weft, passes across them, going over some and under others. Each trip adds one row. title: Why does a story’s setting matter?
answer: The setting is where and when a story happens. Finding a key in an empty school just after closing feels different from finding one in a sunny park at noon. answer: A plot is the set of events that make up a story and the ways they fit together. Imagine someone loses a lunchbox, checks the classroom, follows a clue, and finds it on the soccer field. answer: The narrator is the voice that tells the story. A storyteller who says “I opened the door” can tell you what it felt like to be there. title: Why do fables often use talking animals?
answer: A fable is a short story that suggests a lesson. A small mouse in an old fable helps a much larger lion, showing that size does not decide who can be helpful. Animals in fables can talk, make plans, and behave like people. Their different sizes or habits make the problem easy to picture. A fable can leave you to work out its lesson, or state it plainly at the end.
facts: A fable’s lesson is often called its moral.

title: What is a simile?
answer: A simile puts two unlike things side by side using a word such as “like” or “as.” If you write that a puddle is “as smooth as a mirror,” you help the reader see the water reflecting things around it. The puddle is still water. A good comparison makes one detail clearer. Saying the puddle is “like lunch” might confuse a reader unless the rest of the story explains the connection.
facts: In “the cat crept like a shadow,” the comparison suggests quiet movement.

title: What is a metaphor?
answer: In a metaphor, an author talks about one thing as though it were something else. If someone writes “the moon was a silver coin,” they are comparing the moon’s look with a coin, not describing what the moon is made of. Readers use clues to decide which qualities connect the two things. The comparison can make a sentence do more work than just saying the moon looked round and bright.
facts: A metaphor can compare a feeling or idea as well as a thing you can see.

title: Why do writers give objects feelings?
answer: Personification gives a human action or feeling to something that is not human. The sentence “the sun peeked through the clouds” makes sunlight seem to act like a shy person looking around a corner. The sun does not have eyes. A writer may use that kind of language to make a scene feel playful, calm, or uneasy. It can turn a plain description into something you can imagine right away.
facts: A poem can give a tree human actions, such as waving or whispering.

title: Why repeat the first sound of words?
answer: When nearby words begin with the same sound, the effect is called alliteration. Say “soft snow slipped past” and listen to the repeated s sound. Sound matters more than spelling. The words city and sand begin with the same sound even though they start with different letters. A writer may repeat a sound to draw your ear to a line or make a phrase easier to remember.
facts: The words cat and city do not alliterate with each other, even though they start with the same letter.

title: Why do some words rhyme?
answer: The words light and kite rhyme because their stressed vowel and the sounds after it match. The spelling can be different, as it is in blue and through. Poems and songs may repeat rhymes in a pattern, such as ending the second and fourth lines with matching sounds. Readers can often hear what kind of word might come next. A poem can use rhyme, but it does not have to.

answer: A free verse poem does not have to follow a fixed rhyme pattern or a set number of beats per line. The writer can still plan where each line ends, how sounds repeat, and which words call for a pause. Try reading two versions of the same short poem with the line breaks in different places. You may notice different words even though the poem says exactly the same thing.

title: What is a haiku?
answer: A haiku is a very short poem that began in Japan. It often makes you notice a small moment in nature. A writer might put the sound of a crow beside the sight of an empty branch and let the two details work together. Many English-language classrooms try three lines of five, seven, and five syllables. Traditional Japanese haiku counts Japanese sound units, so poems in English may use other short patterns.
facts: You can write a haiku without using rhyming words.

title: What tells a musician how fast to play?
answer: Tempo is the speed of the beat in music. Imagine walking with a steady drum tap. Fast taps make you take more steps in the same amount of time. Slow taps give you more time between steps. A musician may follow a printed word that says how fast to play, or a number that gives beats per minute. A piece can change tempo while it is being played, which can make it feel as if it is gathering speed or settling down.
facts: Sixty beats per minute gives one beat every second.

title: How do musicians know how loudly to play?
answer: Dynamics tell musicians how loud or soft their music should sound. A group may begin so softly that you can barely hear it, then grow louder until the whole room seems full. That gradual increase is a crescendo. Written music often shows letters such as p for soft or f for loud. A player may make one short note stand out without making the entire song louder.
facts: Musical dynamics are different from tempo, which describes the speed of the beat.

title: What’s the difference between melody and harmony?
answer: The melody is the line of notes you might hum when you remember a song. Harmony comes from notes sounding together or from the way groups of notes change underneath that tune. Imagine one student singing a tune while another holds lower notes that fit with it. You can still follow the tune, but the extra notes change how it feels. A piece can have more than one melody that fits together.
facts: A chord is a group of notes heard as a unit.

title: What happens inside a piano when you press a key?
answer: Press a key on an acoustic piano and it moves a small hammer hidden inside. The hammer strikes one or more strings tuned for that note and quickly pulls away. The strings vibrate, and a wooden soundboard helps spread the sound through the air. A padded part usually lands against the strings again when you let go of the key. A pedal can keep many of those pads raised so sounds last longer.

title: How does a violin make a sound?
answer: A violin player draws a bow across a string to make it vibrate. A small wooden bridge carries some of that motion into the body of the violin, which helps send sound into the room. The player can press a string down with a finger to shorten the part that vibrates. A shorter part usually makes a higher note. A violin can also sound when the player plucks a string.

title: Why does a cello sound lower than a violin?
answer: A cello has long strings and a large wooden body. Its strings are tuned to make lower notes than the strings of a violin, and the body helps those sounds reach the air. A person usually plays a cello seated, with the instrument standing between their knees and an endpin resting on the floor. Like a violin player, they can bow or pluck the strings and press them to change the notes.

title: Why is a double bass so big?
answer: The double bass is the largest of the string instruments usually found in an orchestra. Its long, thick strings can move back and forth slowly enough to give it very low notes. In an orchestra, players can move a bow across the strings. In jazz and other kinds of music, they often pluck the strings with their fingers. title: How does a guitar change notes?
answer: A guitar string makes a sound when you pluck it and it vibrates. On an acoustic guitar, those vibrations move into the body, which helps spread the sound. The small bars across the long neck are called frets. Press a string just behind a fret and the part that can vibrate gets shorter. Shortening the string raises the pitch, so two presses on the same string can make different notes.

When the player opens or closes holes with keys, the air inside acts as if it has a different length. That helps change the note. title: Why does a clarinet need a reed?
answer: On a clarinet, a thin strip called a reed sits against a mouthpiece. When a player blows, the reed flexes quickly and sets the air in the tube vibrating. Fingers and keys open and close holes to help change the note. A player can also change how they blow to play notes in different parts of the instrument’s range. The same clarinet can sound quite soft or strong.

answer: An oboe player blows between two very thin pieces of cane. They are tied together near the base and can move quickly against one another at the tip. That movement helps create a vibration in the long tube. The player uses keys and fingers to cover or uncover holes to change notes. An oboe’s sound can stand out even when its part is fairly quiet.

Push it outward and the air path grows longer, which can make the note lower. Move the slide smoothly while keeping the sound going and some notes can glide between pitches. answer: Timpani are bowl-shaped drums with skins or plastic heads stretched across their tops. Strike the drum with a soft-headed stick, and its stretched surface makes a clear note. title: What does checkmate mean in chess?
answer: In chess, a king is in check when one of the other player’s pieces attacks the square it is on. The player has to answer the threat. They might move the king to a safe square, capture the threatening piece, or place another piece between them. When none of those choices can make the king safe, it is checkmate. The game ends before anyone actually takes the king off the board.
facts: If the player has no legal move and the king is safe from check, the game is a draw called stalemate.

title: What changes when a checker becomes a king?
answer: In English draughts, often called checkers, each player starts with pieces on the dark squares of a board. An ordinary piece moves one square diagonally forward to an empty space. It can capture an opposing piece by jumping diagonally forward over it to the empty square just beyond. When a piece reaches the farthest row on the other side, it becomes a king. From then on, it can move and capture diagonally forward or backward.

A stone or connected group needs empty points next to it, along the lines. If the other player occupies the last of those neighboring empty points, they take the group off the board.
